I have added to BallyAlley.com the six-page, handwritten Bally BASIC type-in program listing and documentation for "Life IV" by Matt Giwer from 1980.

https://ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#Life_IV_Matt_Giwer_Type-In

As far as I'm aware, this program has not been archived from tape yet, nor do I think we have it available to us. Paul, could you check on this fact for me?

"Life IV" by Matt Giwer is a Bally BASIC program first advertised in ARCADIAN 2, no. 6 (Apr. 25, 1980): 56. It was originally available on cassette or open reel tape with documentation for $5.50.  There sure were not many programs sold on open reel tapes!

Matt, the programmer from Annandale, Virginia, writes, "Enclosed is the description, listing, documentation, initial data and an ad [for 'Life IV']. Not only is it slow but addicting. I let it run overnight. Every time I've tried to improve the program there is some error in functioning that is traceable to the cursor. Without the cursor the game is less interesting. A machine language version is needed.

"Note I use a 30x35 array and a 60x70 is possible. The entire display array could be used to store 1s and 0s. [...] The screen is split left and right to display the present and future generation. The current generation is scanned with each location cursor provided for reference."

There were quite a few "Game of Life" programs written for both Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC.  I find people's interest in these programs engrossing, for, to me, these BASIC versions are very-much like slow video art programs.

Enjoy!

https://ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#Find_Yogi_and_Ever_Changing_Cross_Type-In

This four-page document contains a typed letter to Bob Fabris and two BASIC programs: a game called "M-I - Find Yogi" and video art called "M-II - Ever Changing Cross." It's unclear if these programs are for Bally BASIC or AstroBASIC. These seem to be early versions of the programs. For example, "Ever Changing Cross" was later expanded for Blue Ram BASIC.

These are brief notes, which I've tried to make clear without changing the original text too much, from the type-in listing for "M-II - Ever Changing Cross:" "A short but attractive program. Design many attractive variations can be made of this program by changing BOX parameters. [...] Program could easily be changed to input different BOX and STEP sizes from the keyboard. The variations and different designs are extensive."

Keeping track of which of Stanley Kendall's programs have been archived from tape is difficult, because he seems to have often changed his programs, made updates to them and ported them to different versions of BASIC for the Astrocade.  Also, Stan was quite prolific on the Astrocade.  Here are some of his video art programs that I've uploaded to YouTube in the past:

https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=stanley+kendall+video+art+astrocade

Enjoy!

https://ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#Record_Keeping_and_Big_Six_Gambler_Type-In

This four-page document was probably sent to Bob Fabris, the editor of the "Arcadian" newsletter, sometime in the summer of 1984 after one of the programs was updated. It contains a letter and two BASIC programs for Bally BASIC/AstroBASIC.

The first title is properly called "Record Keeping for AstroBASIC with Blue RAM Memory." According to the notes in the BASIC listing, this program was previously known as "Home Improvements" and was written on April 21, 1984 and revised for the 16K Blue RAM on July 9, 1984. Allen writes, "Use this program to store and retrieve auto costs, home improvements, computer software, record albums, etc. It is written to use the added 8K of space accessible by AstroBASIC. This could be modified to suit many needs. This program will also run in Bally BASIC and [Blue Ram BASIC]."

The full name of the second program is "Big Six Gambler for One," which was written on February 2, 1983. Allen converted this game from "More BASIC Computer Games" by David Ahl. Allen says, "I have altered the original concept only slightly in this AstroBASIC version." The game starts by asking you how many numbers you want to bet on. You can use up to three.

I don't think that either of these programs has been archived from tape.

I think that Allen Skaggs used to be a member of this group.  Allen, if you're still reading these posts, then do you have any comments about these two programs?

Enjoy!

This year saw a remarkable surge in BASIC computing and 8-bit machines for the annual BASIC challenge hosted by Logiker: https://logiker.com/Vintage-Computing-Christmas-Challenge-2022  The for-fun challenge was to recreate an eight-pointed star of asterisks in as minimal coding as necessary as you can see in the screenshot at the link above. A separate casual category was “wild” where it was more about creativity or experimentation rather than optimization or replication. I couldn’t help but think of Bally as an interesting early BASIC system. With the limited time I had this past week, I enjoyed becoming more familiar with Astro BASIC’s limitations and capabilities.

 

I wound up producing an endlessly altering snowflake drawing for the “wild” category. The variations it generates can create a real glistening look to them, even with speckled snow frosted across it at times! This was the only contribution done on the Bally platform, and makes an appearance around 18:20 of the official rundown video by Logiker: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xVKEaRogw-s <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xVKEaRogw-s&t=1101s> &t=1101s – Logiker told me that he had never heard of Bally until my submission so wound up researching about it and was intrigued. If I had stuck with the original concept of using text characters to generate the snowflake, Bally would struggle since it is unable to achieve the 17 text rows needed on a single screen without scrolling even in Blue RAM BASIC and the 3x5 character set. But creative use of the LINE command made it look even nicer anyhow 😊

 

While working to clean-up and repair the original Bally keypad to help reduce key bounce, I dove into the emulation side of things to test my ideas out. Adam has made some excellent and thorough guides on his BallyAlley YouTube <https://www.youtube.com/@ballyalley/search?query=emulation>  Channel, which are still every bit applicable even to the latest version of MAME. I went a step beyond the keyboard mapping and reskinned a dedicated 24 keypad (Genovation ControlPad CP24) with a custom-created overlay set, some $7 woodgrain liner and even added a 3D printed Bally logo. For the key overlays (sized to 0.55 inches squared) I made it as versatile as possible for the major utilities. This includes Machine Language Manager, Calculator and Bally BASIC. I arranged these all as high DPI/PPI layout for printing on 4x6 photo paper. Then cut each square out to include on the control pad. With its software I was able to create a profile that matches the MAME mappings while physically matching the Bally specs albeit more comfortable to use. You can see a photo of this keypad attached, or at the video below. Separately from this, I also began developing a front-end overlay for the MAME system and have a proof-of-concept functional on my machine that allows clicking any one of the options or feeding entire lines in to serve up to MAME, which greatly speeds up testing and allows more direct development work within MAME, screenshot as well—it will be sometime next year before I will have it polished up or instructions on how to use it.

 

Attached are some screenshots of my Bally snowflake running, as well as the typed-in source code that I authored. A written interpretation of the code is also below (the tilde character correlates to the asterisk array in Bally):

 

1 .VCC 2022: MATT PILZ

10 BC=72;FC=0;D=1;S=3;CLEAR

20 FOR I = 0 TO 6

30 IF I>1 IF I<6 N=(I+1)/2

40 @(I) = 1 + RM

50 ~(I+4) = @(I)*(-1)

60 IF I>3 ~(I-4)=@(I)

70 NEXT I

80 FOR U=2 TO 21 STEP S

90 XY=U;N=0;M=1

100 FOR I = 0 TO 15

110 IF I>7 N=-1;M=N

120 LINE ~(I+(8*N))*U*M,@(I+(8*N))*U*M,D

130 IF FC<7 FC=FC+1;BC=BC-8

140 NEXT I

150 NEXT U

160 D=RND(4);S=RND(10)+1

170 GOTO 80

 

It does a lot of cryptic-seeming things just cause I was having fun factoring and refactoring ideas. What I like about the way Bally saves to cassette is how it writes the entire screen RAM that doubles as BASIC RAM, so for this demonstration I was able to run the program, halt it when a particular design had appeared, alter BC and FC values and then save to tape. When loaded, it displays this nice red/green preview before even running it, which is nice. I then do a smooth transition from that red value to a blue and similar approach for the foreground color, to give it a subtle fade-in effect as soon as it is run. The background color could easily pulsate or subtly change over time to complete this sort of screensaver-like program.

 

The creative appearance of the snowflake, which at times will make speckled snow particles and other times will add or remove shimmer and layers, is all made possible by randomizing the mode of the line draw to foreground, background, inverted/erase… This coupled with slight randomness in step size and iterations leads to a lot of cool possibilities. I use both available arrays to store the x/y pattern needed to draw the design, I essentially calculate half of it and then inverse it to draw the other half. The line command and overall coordinate system was new to me, with 0,0 being the origin point and the line destination always being relative to that point (and with a start as stored in XY). One aspect to watch out for when using the @ array, which starts where the BASIC code ends in memory, as noted in the manual: “It's Important to remember that If you modify your program and make It longer, you will cover up the data you had stored in the memory area your program expanded into.” So in retrospect and due to some funnies that occurred as I was experimenting, I could’ve just stuck with the * array for it all to ensure any alterations were far removed from where the array data began.

First to type it all out on the Bally, most often using the native calculator keypad, to verify functionality. Then having to LIST it and manually transcribe and compare it back by pen or typewriter/PC for the circulation. Other platforms and newsletters had it easier by enabling dot matrix printers and the ability to LLIST directly to it to send to newsletters, but I found even then they suffer from poor readability when embedded in newsletters.

19897:
Following up to recent discussions about type-in digitization efforts, I
have done a full conversion of the remaining Seebree's Computing (Tim Hayes)
type-in program, Munch.

 

It is made available as both 300 baud and 2000 baud, with source, binaries
and WAV files attached including the original and a subtly modified version
to fix certain bugs. The 300 baud version has a load time of 2:11, while the
2000 baud version takes only 0:17.

 

DESCRIPTION FROM ORIGINAL PAPER:
https://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/sebree/munch.pdf 

 

This game is very easy in concept. After reading the on screen instructions,
press your trigger to start. When your cookie is on the screen, move the
cursor (flashing box) to where you want to start eating. The object is to
get 2,000 points without eating the poison raisin, which is randomly placed
in the cookie. If you win, the computer will show you where the poison
raisin was. Don't press your trigger down constantly because your bites
won't be big enough. The joystick is used to move around, and the trigger is
used to take a bite. If you just want to see where the poison raisin is,
enter 'GOTO 300'.

 

STORY AND INSTRUCTIONS FROM IN-GAME TITLE SCREEN:

 

An ex-friend gave you a cookie with a poison raisin in it. You decide to eat
this harmless looking cookie. (Until you croak after it's too late.) Use the
joystick to move your mouth around, press the trigger to munch away!! If you
get more than 2,000 points, you win the game, if you're not poisoned by
then!! Press trigger to start.

 

MY MODIFIED VERSION CHANGES:

 

* Restored title screen sound when playing multiple rounds.

* Fixed HUD text so it doesn't break game border when playing.

* Added constraints so you can't eat outside the bounds of the cookie.

* Typo correction

 

MY SHORT REVIEW:

 

Similar in spirit to minesweeper, except without any clues about where that
poison raisin might reside! I enjoyed seeing the use of subtract mode
drawing to emulate eating the cookie, with every press of the trigger the
area over your square will vanish. It has a mildly creative title screen and
if you eat the poison it plays a classic ominous tune. However there are
some oversights with gameplay in that you can eat from the same spot
endlessly, though in my modified version I at least made it so you can't eat
out of bounds. In the original you can move the cursor anywhere on the
screen even far away from the cookie, and each trigger press will still
score points. The game has a definitive ending if you reach over 2,000
points, and you receive a random scoring of 5-8 per bite. This means every
game will require at least 250-500 bites to complete. Since it shows the
score at all times, I could see this being enjoyable competing against
another to see who can get the highest score. You can adjust the score
increments by changing line 145, or the max required score by changing line
156. 

 

ARCHIVING NOTES:

 

This was done mostly as part of my continued efforts in creating a front-end
interface hook for MAME emulation, which I had begun when making the
Snowflake program last month.  I made a lot of improvements on that project
and hope to be able to share a demonstration in the near future, it is
becoming quite versatile as a modern solution.

 

I typed in the hand-written code into an ordinary text editor, and then was
able to pass it through my front-end to parse and auto-type it into MAME. If
you look at the 2000 baud source code you'll notice it is quite different
from the required 300 baud code used in TXT2PRG and a closer one-to-one
comparison to the actual code. The structure in my syntax is more forgiving
in that it doesn't care what you capitalize and isn't as picky about spaces
(but still desirable to include them around any reserved words). And you use
the native ASCII characters for arrows and division symbols directly (which
in the front-end converts for you automatically when typing normally, with
some special key cases such as arrow keys via the 2/4/6/8 on Number Pad). I
have made solid progress on this as part of the type-in here as a test
subject, to the point where I was able to feed it the 2000 baud source code
as seen in the ZIP file and it output all of it via MAME in 2 minutes 17
seconds, approximately the same speed as :INPUT demands at 300 baud. From
there I was able to save a digital cassette of it, which made a 0:17
duration after trimming the silence.

 

The only incompatibility the original listing had with AstroBASIC / 2000
Baud was the use of the ":return" command at the start. This was used in the
original Bally BASIC to physically stop the cassette interface, which my
understanding means if you loaded via ":INPUT;RUN" it'd load the app, run it
automatically and auto-shut off the cassette interface. I left this command
in tact for the 300 baud, but omitted it from the 2000 baud versions.

 

I was curious about the TXT2PRG system for generating 300 baud type-ins so
subsequently converted my 2000 baud original code into the necessary syntax
for 300 baud. Again you can compare the differences in the included text
file sources. You can see especially in the title screen source lines that
the 2000 baud source is more direct, as the title uses a lot of arrow
symbols that must be manually typed as "right right right" etc. for TXT2PRG
compatibility. It was not too complicated and I like that the program checks
for some obvious problems while building the binary. It ran fine on Windows
11. I moved the 300 baud source into its folder, then ran the command:
txt2prg munch.txt munch.prg (you could also add the directory to your system
path so you could execute it from any folder against any compatible source).
To do the final WAV conversion required using DOSBox, since the KCS utility
isn't supported on 64-bit machines. Within DOSBox, I mounted a directory to
the location of that program, which I first moved to a simple directory
(e.g., "mount e c:\temp\txt2prg\" within DOSBox). Then I used the command
KCS -M -L5 -P50 MUNCH.PRG and it created a matching WAV file within a minute
or two. Be careful with long filenames as within DOSBox they are constrained
to 8 characters or otherwise end up with tilde reductions, so it's easiest
to name the PRG file something short before converting to WAV and then
convert back afterward. I tested the 300 baud on the physical machine to
verify functionality.

 

That's all for now, enjoy!

What have we got on the discussion group and on BallyAlley.com.  Well, let's take a peek and find out.

I quickly pulled this list together which features Dale's programs.  I know that I overlooked some useful links, so please post to this thread when you see anything that I should have listed here.

Let's begin with five topics:

1) An interview with Dale Low of Astrogames

Here is the interview with Dale Low that Paul posted to this group on August 22, 2021.  It is this interview that lead directly to Paul getting some tapes from Dale.

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/85056855#18268

Here is the interview on BallyAlley.com.  You may find this page enlightening, as there are other interviews with people on this page who created Astrocade software.

https://ballyalley.com/ballyalley/interviews/interviews.html#Interview_with_Dale_Low_of_Astrogames

2) "Review of Astrogames, Tapes A1 and A2," by Kevin O'Neill (December 1983)

This is a review of seven games for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade that are on tapes A1 and A2 from Astrogames. This review first appeared in the Outlet, Product Review Column in NIAGARA B.U.G. BULLETIN, 1, no. 7 (December 1984): 25-26.

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/reviews/Astrogames_Review/Astrogames%20Review.html

3) "Astrocade 'The Game Player' Reviews Compilation" by Michael Prosise ("Arcadian," October 7, 1982 - October 31, 1984.)

"The Game Player" was a review column from the "Arcadian" newsletter that ran for twenty-one columns. It reviewed a total of thirty-nine games, only five of which were cartridges. The rest were all games that were sold on tape.  Astrogames' tapes A1 and A2, containing seven total games, are reviewed:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/reviews/astrocade_reviews.txt

4) "Metropolitan Attack!" Uncredited, but probably by Dale Low. (ARCADIAN 6, no. 11 (Oct. 31, 1984): 99-128.)

This is a Missile Command clone written for "AstroBASIC."

Michael Prosise reviews the game (briefly) in his December 1983 Game Player column: "Metro Attack. Three cheers for Dale Low! This is a game I could really get excited about! It is the best Missile Command simulation I have ever seen. It contains selectable levels, turns, players, bonus energy points, whew! In short, this game has it all! My personal favorite."

See the program's notes for many additional details about this program, including how it came to be archived.

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_i-p/programs_i-p.html#MetropolitanAttackAB

5) "Maze Avenger" by Dale Low (ARCADIAN, 6, no. 11/12 (October 31, 1984): 100.)

Note that the Arcadian newsletter provided no instructions on how to play this game, but plenty are provided here.

"Maze Avenger" is a maze game where the player's character creeps ever so slowly around the maze shooting objects that are not at all easily identifiable. When the character shoots all of the objects on the screen then the player advances to the next level. The player can be hit by-- well-- SOMETHING and it causes the player to be unable to shoot and also to be able to pass through walls.

When this program was typed in, we discovered that this game had problems as-printed in the "Arcadian" newsletter.  Richard Degler fixed the program and also made a commented disassembly listing of the Z80 source code and BASIC listing that are well worth a read for those who are interested in hybrid BASIC/ML programs for AstroBASIC.

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/Maze%20Avenger/Maze%20Avenger%20(1984)(Dale%20Low).zip

This should be enough information to whet anyone's appetite for information about Dale Low and Astrogames.  There are at least a few archived AstroBASIC programs by Dale that I didn't list here, such as "Control 30" and "Pac*Man." The final hi-res Astrocade project continues to progress slowly. Operation and compatibility issues had to be resolved. The project was placed on hold numerous times, so other projects could be completed.

SIMPLIFIED HI-RES DRAM Astrocade

For example, a 2nd wire wrapped (WW) low/high-res static RAM (SRAM) board 1 was built and tested.

I decided to install this 2nd board into my original hi-res dynamic RAM (DRAM) Astrocade. The original WW board for this Astrocade is shown in the attached Photo 1.

The original board has multiple schemes on it. The board has way too many chips on it. A board failure could be "messy" to diagnose. Breaking down the schemes into 2 boards would be better. The full size matrix keyboard interface and the Z80 DART schemes will be dropped. The original board will be tore down for parts.

The upgrade for this hi-res DRAM Astrocade is really in the form of simplicity.

For example, the original board utilizes 32 chips of hi-res DRAM. Now, I view the hi-res DRAM scheme as obsolete. The new board chip count reduces the old 32 chip requirement to only 6 chips (4 SRAM + 74F138 + 74F86).

The old board requires a triple 5v/12v/-5v power supply plus a step down power transformer. The new board requires only a single 5v power supply.

A dual 5v/12v power supply was installed in the Viper cabinet (no step down xfmr required). The 12v supply is used only for the power audio amp, which can drive a single 8 ohm remote speaker.

Attached is Photo 2 showing the new board and dual power supply mounted underneath the Astrocade console, which can swing up and back, away from the add-under Viper cabinet.

The User ROM/RAM and low/hi-res auto select schemes will be installed later on a 2nd smaller WW board 2, which will be mounted on top of the new board 1.

The original 24 pin ribbon cable (RC) socket on the modified for hi-res Astrocade motherboard was replaced with a new 28 pin RC socket. Now, all 28 required motherboard tapped signal lines for hi-res operation are connected to the new board 1 via the 28 pin RC connect. This frees up the motherboard 50 pin expansion for optional hardware plug-ins.

This motherboard is now compatible, for use as a diagnostic tool, with the upcoming final hi-res Astrocade. I actually have a 3rd compatible modified for hi-res motherboard, but it has a failure on it and will be diagnosed at a later time.

The newly installed low/hi-res WW board 1 runs perfect. In the future, the motherboard and board 1 can be removed and placed flat on a table for easy diagnostic access.

NEW HI-RES GRAPHICS BOARD

Another project recently completed was the bread boarding and testing of a new optional hi-res graphics board. This is not the hi-res graphics pattern transfer board announced some time ago, which will be bread boarded and tested later.

You will see this new graphics board operating in an upcoming YouTube video. This new video is expected to be released several weeks (?) from now, once the all new hi-res graphics are programmed. That will be fun creating new hi-res graphics.
